ETSII | UPM — GenAI for Management – Hanna Lanéus
Task 1 — Inventory & Initial Scan
Document Analysis and Organisational Synthesis · Corpus: T01-DocsSet (31 documents)
1. Purpose
This report establishes the boundaries of the knowledge domain contained in the inherited document set. Before any synthesis can take place, the organisation must know what it actually holds: how many documents, of what kind, published where and when, and which analytical tools they bring to the problem of furnace scheduling and energy efficiency in steelmaking.
2. Method
All 31 PDF files were programmatically unpacked and their text layers extracted. Embedded PDF metadata (title, author, subject, keywords, creation date) was read where present and reconciled against the first two pages of each document, which carry the authoritative title block, author affiliations, journal reference and abstract. Where embedded metadata was missing or corrupted, bibliographic data was recovered manually from the rendered front matter. Keywords were taken from the authors' own keyword lists where available, and otherwise derived from the abstract.
3. Corpus at a glance
Three observations follow immediately from this profile. First, the archive is entirely external literature — it contains no proprietary plant records, so it can define what is possible but not what our specific furnaces currently do. Second, the temporal spread is deliberate rather than accidental: the earlier material (2016–2020) is dominated by mathematical scheduling models, while everything from 2023 onward is dominated by learning-based and digital-twin methods. Third, the corpus is densely concentrated on one industry — steel, and within it reheating and heat-treatment furnaces — which means it is narrow but directly relevant.
4. Full metadata inventory
5. Initial scan: what tools does this archive bring to the problem?
A first pass over the abstracts shows five families of method present in the set. These are named here only to bound the domain; they are mapped properly in Task 2.
Mathematical and metaheuristic scheduling. MILP models, polynomial-time algorithms, online algorithms, and population metaheuristics (NSGA-II, MOPSO, migrating birds, grey wolf, matheuristics) applied to furnace charging, batching and rolling sequences.
Uncertainty handling. Robust optimisation, proactive scheduling with buffers, fuzzy characterisation of uncertain heating values, time-series forecasting of job release, and reactive rescheduling under disturbance.
Deep reinforcement learning. Single-agent and multi-agent DRL for energy scheduling, demand response and spot-market participation, including recent LLM-assisted reward design.
Digital twins and data-driven prediction. High-fidelity twins of walking-beam reheating furnaces, IoT-based twin frameworks, and surrogate predictors such as GA-BP models of energy consumption per tonne.
Explainability, trust and human factors. XAI for genetic algorithms and for DRL, counterfactual explanation, transparency reviews of planning tools, Industry 5.0 human-centric scheduling, and process-safety perspectives on automation versus augmentation.
6. Immediate findings and gaps
The archive is coherent. Despite being described as scattered fragments, the set has a clear centre of gravity: energy-efficient scheduling of steel furnaces under uncertainty. There is no off-topic material.
The three technologies named in the brief are all present and well evidenced. DRL appears in six documents, digital twins in six, and explainable AI in six, with several documents bridging two of the three.
Energy is framed in two incompatible ways. Some documents minimise physical consumption (GJ per tonne, idle energy); others minimise energy cost against time-varying electricity prices. These are not the same objective and will need reconciling.
Two structural gaps are visible at this stage. There is no document addressing implementation economics, change management or capital cost, and none reporting a long-run production deployment — nearly all validation is by simulation or single case study.
No internal baseline exists. Because the archive holds no plant data, any recommendation derived from it will require a measurement phase before targets can be committed to.
7. Conclusion
The boundaries of the knowledge domain are now established. The organisation holds 31 peer-reviewed documents spanning eleven years, unified by the problem of scheduling energy-intensive steel furnaces under uncertainty, and offering five distinct families of method with which to attack it. The archive is fit for purpose as a source of technical direction, but it is silent on cost, on organisational readiness and on our own operational baseline. Task 2 proceeds to map the internal structure of this domain.

ETSII | UPM — GenAI for Management – Hanna Lanéus
Task 2 — Topographical Mapping
Hierarchical topic tree and cross-reference network of the 31-document corpus
1. Purpose and method
Task 1 established what the archive contains. This report establishes how it is organised: where knowledge is concentrated, where it is isolated, and which documents act as structural bridges between otherwise separate bodies of work. Each document was assigned a primary theme on the basis of its stated contribution, and secondary assignments were made where a document makes a substantive contribution to a second theme. Documents were then linked to one another where they share a method, an object of study or an objective function. The resulting structure is presented first as a hierarchical tree and then as a network.
2. Hierarchical topic tree
Document numbers refer to the inventory in the Task 1 report. Counts of core documents sum to 29; documents 13 and 31 are counted as bridging and are assigned to two clusters each.
3. Cross-reference network
The figure below plots the same structure as a network. Node size distinguishes clusters from documents; colour indicates cluster membership; edges connect documents to the clusters they contribute to, and clusters to one another where a methodological relationship exists.
Figure 1 — Cross-reference network of the corpus. Bridging documents (13, 31) appear between two cluster hubs.
4. Where knowledge is concentrated
Cluster A is the deepest and the oldest. Nine documents, mostly 2016–2021, treat furnace scheduling as a well-posed optimisation problem. The organisation is therefore well supplied with formulations, constraint sets and solution algorithms that are mature, auditable and reproducible.
Furnace-specific physical detail is concentrated in A and D. Documents 1, 10, 14, 15 and 23 carry the constraints that actually bind a reheating furnace: minimum heating time, maximum residence time, charging capacity, billet geometry, deterioration of heating efficiency. This is the corpus's most valuable and least substitutable content.
Energy cost, as opposed to energy quantity, is concentrated in C. Documents 5, 9 and 21 are the only ones that treat electricity price as a decision variable and connect scheduling to demand response and spot markets.
5. Where knowledge is isolated
Cluster E is peripheral. Five of its six documents attach only to E. Explainability is discussed as a general property of planning tools (6), of genetic algorithms (4) or of process operations (25), but almost never of the specific furnace-scheduling systems described in clusters A to D. The corpus knows that trust matters and separately knows how to schedule furnaces, but it rarely does both at once.
Document 13 is a single point of failure in the map. It is the only link between DRL and explainability. Any strategy that depends on deploying an explainable learned controller rests, in this archive, on one conference paper from 2022.
Document 25 (process safety) and document 16 (Industry 5.0) are the most isolated nodes overall. They raise the governance and human-oversight questions that a high-stakes furnace environment demands, but they are not connected to any scheduling model in the set.
Demand response and metallurgical constraint modelling never meet. Clusters C and A share no document. The market-facing work abstracts the furnace away; the furnace-specific work ignores the price signal.
6. What the structure reveals
The map shows a corpus organised along a single implicit axis running from computational rigour to organisational acceptability. Cluster A sits at one end: precise, constrained, verifiable, but static and blind to price. Cluster E sits at the other: attentive to operators, regulators and trust, but computationally empty. Clusters C and D sit between them, and the bridging documents 13 and 31 mark the only paths that currently cross the gap.
The practical consequence is that the archive does not contain a ready-made solution. It contains the components of one, distributed across clusters that were never designed to be combined, with the joins between them evidenced by single documents rather than by bodies of work. Task 3 examines the specific disagreements along this axis; Task 4 attempts the combination.

ETSII | UPM — GenAI for Management – Hanna Lanéus
Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence
Contrasting approaches within the key sub-topics identified in Task 2
1. Purpose
A map shows where the material sits; it does not show where it disagrees. This report drills into the sub-topics identified in Task 2 and sets the competing approaches against one another. The disagreements matter because each one corresponds to a decision the organisation cannot avoid making. Five substantive tensions were identified.
2. The five tensions
1. How should the schedule be computed?
The exact-methods literature is confident but narrow: document 1 achieves polynomial time only by restricting the machine-mode model, and document 28 reports a 29.57% energy reduction from a single no-idle constraint under laboratory conditions with up to 200 jobs and eight machines. The DRL literature is broader but softer: document 9 addresses genuine exogenous uncertainty from electricity prices and on-site renewables, which no MILP in the set attempts, but validates in simulation. Notably, document 20 is an admission against interest — it exists because reward design and state representation in DRL are unsolved enough to require large language models and human feedback to patch them.
Trade-off forced on the organisation: optimality guarantees and auditability against real-time adaptivity and the ability to absorb uncertainty that was never modelled.
2. Should uncertainty be absorbed before or during execution?
Document 29 formulates robust optimisation for the hot strip mill precisely because deterministic models are ineffective under processing-time uncertainty. Document 2 goes further, pre-compressing processing times to buy robustness against machine breakdown. The opposing camp treats this as waste: document 3 forecasts job release times and reschedules online, while document 18 builds a three-layer architecture that detects disturbances and adaptively reconfigures the schedule. Document 11 is the most radical, discarding central planning altogether in favour of agents trading in a virtual market.
Trade-off forced on the organisation: schedule stability, which operators and downstream customers value, against responsiveness and the avoidance of permanently reserved slack.
3. What exactly is being minimised?
This is the sharpest divergence in the corpus, and the two camps share no document. Document 14 predicts heat energy consumption per tonne to 94.7% accuracy and treats that quantity as the target. Document 9 treats the same furnace as an asset to be scheduled against the electricity spot market. The two objectives can actively conflict: shifting a heat to a cheap overnight price window may require holding a slab longer, which increases physical consumption and scale loss. Document 22 is the closest the archive comes to reconciliation, treating tardiness and energy cost as an explicit bi-objective Pareto problem rather than pretending one dominates.
Trade-off forced on the organisation: a decarbonisation objective measured in energy units against a financial objective measured in currency; optimising either alone will degrade the other.
4. Must the system be explainable, and at what price?
The performance camp does not argue against explanation; it simply does not raise the question. The explainability camp argues that this is the failure mode. Document 13 states the problem directly: black-box models reduce user trust in machine-learning-based production planning and control. Document 6 frames opacity as producing results that are highly accurate yet incomprehensible. Document 8 offers the most operationally useful answer, generating counterfactual explanations that tell a planner what would have had to differ for another schedule to be chosen. Document 25 raises the stakes for a high-temperature environment, asking whether the goal should be artificial intelligence or intelligence augmentation for safer process operation.
Trade-off forced on the organisation: the highest-performing methods are the least transparent, and in a safety-critical furnace environment the transparent-but-weaker system may deliver more realised benefit than the opaque-but-stronger one it replaces.
5. What should a digital twin actually be?
Document 10 argues that the absence of digital representation is exactly why existing optimisation schemes deviate badly on implementation, and builds a high-fidelity twin of parallel walking-beam furnaces to close that gap. Document 19 extends this to an IoT framework spanning hot and cold rolling, explicitly to break the information silos between stages. Against this, document 14 obtains 94.7% accuracy from a genetic-algorithm-optimised neural network trained on actual production data, with none of the mechanistic modelling effort. Document 31 shows the twin serving a third purpose entirely: as a live training and execution environment for a Deep-Q-Learning policy.
Trade-off forced on the organisation: modelling cost, integration time and calibration effort against accuracy, extrapolation beyond observed conditions, and the ability to reason about conditions the plant has never encountered.
3. What the divergence tells us
The five tensions are not independent. They resolve into a single structural choice: the corpus offers one family of methods that is rigorous, constrained, transparent and static, and another that is adaptive, market-aware, powerful and opaque. Every attempt in the archive to take one side wholesale leaves a visible weakness on the other.
Three consequences follow for the organisation. First, no single document in this set can be adopted as a blueprint, because each optimises within one camp. Second, the tensions are resolvable in principle, and the bridging documents identified in Task 2 show how: a twin can host a learned policy (31), an explanation layer can be fitted to a learned controller (13), and physics constraints can be embedded inside a DRL formulation (5). Third, the objective conflict in tension 3 is the one that cannot be engineered away and must be settled as a management decision before any system is specified.
Task 4 re-converges these positions into a single architecture that assigns each method to the layer where its weakness is least damaging.
Position | Argued by | Claim
Model-based optimisation | 1, 22, 23, 28, 12, 15 | Formulate the furnace problem explicitly and solve it with exact methods or metaheuristics. Solutions are feasible by construction, bounded in quality, and inspectable.
Learned policy (DRL) | 5, 9, 20, 21, 31 | Train an agent to map plant state to scheduling actions. The policy reacts in milliseconds and improves with exposure to uncertainty rather than requiring it to be modelled in advance.
Position | Argued by | Claim
Proactive / robust | 2, 29, 24, 7 | Build protection into the plan in advance — buffers, robust counterparts, fuzzy bounds — so that the schedule survives disturbance without being changed.
Reactive / dynamic | 3, 11, 18 | Accept that plans will break, and invest instead in detecting disturbance and rescheduling quickly.
Position | Argued by | Claim
Physical energy consumption | 1, 14, 15, 23, 28, 30 | Reduce gigajoules per tonne, idle energy and residence time. The gain is permanent, measurable at the furnace, and counts toward decarbonisation.
Energy cost and market position | 9, 21, 5, 22, 24 | Reduce the money paid for energy by shifting load to cheap periods and selling flexibility back through demand response.
Position | Argued by | Claim

Explainability as a precondition | 13, 4, 8, 6, 25 | An unexplained schedule will not be trusted, and an untrusted schedule will be overridden, so opacity destroys the benefit before it is realised.
Position | Argued by | Claim

ETSII | UPM — GenAI for Management – Hanna Lanéus
Task 4 — Integrative Synthesis
A unified organisational blueprint combining DRL, digital twins and XAI within metallurgical constraints
1. The synthesis principle
Task 3 established that the corpus divides into a rigorous, transparent, static family of methods and an adaptive, market-aware, opaque one. The instinct to choose between them is wrong. The two families fail in different places and on different time horizons, which means they can be layered rather than traded off.
The principle adopted here is separation of concerns by time horizon and by authority. Slow, verifiable, constraint-bound methods own the envelope of what is permissible. Fast, learned methods own the choices made inside that envelope. Explanation and human authority sit above both. Under this arrangement, the weakness of each method is contained by the layer beneath it: the DRL agent cannot produce a metallurgically unsafe schedule because the planner's constraints bound its action space, and the planner cannot leave money on the table because the agent is free to move within the band it defines.
2. The layered blueprint
Read upward, the stack answers a single question at each level: what is happening (L0), what will happen (L1), what is allowed (L2), what is best right now (L3), why (L4), and who decides (L5).
3. How the blueprint resolves each tension
4. Metallurgical constraints as the binding layer
The single most important design decision is that metallurgical constraints are enforced structurally, not learned. They are encoded in L2 and applied as a feasibility mask on the action space of L3. The agent is never in a position to trade quality against cost, because the actions that would do so are not available to it.
5. Implementation sequence
Phase 1 — Instrument and measure (0–6 months). Deploy IoT data capture and build the furnace twin. Establish the energy baseline in GJ per tonne, which the archive cannot supply. Deliverable: a validated twin and a defensible baseline.
Phase 2 — Deterministic planner (6–12 months). Implement L2 against real constraints. Run in advisory mode alongside current practice. This phase alone is expected to capture the idle-energy and no-idle gains reported in documents 1, 23 and 28, with no black-box component and therefore minimal adoption risk.
Phase 3 — Explanation and human integration (9–15 months, overlapping). Build L4 and L5 before the learned controller arrives, not after. Planners become familiar with machine-generated reasoning while the system is still fully deterministic, which is the cheapest moment to establish trust.
Phase 4 — Learned control (15–24 months). Train the L3 agent inside the twin, then release it shadow-mode, then within a narrow band of the L2 plan, widening only as measured performance and planner acceptance justify it.
Phase 5 — Market participation (24 months onward). Extend L3 to demand response and spot-market bidding once intra-shift flexibility is proven and quantified.
6. What this blueprint does not solve
Three limitations should be stated plainly, because the archive cannot address them and no architecture can conceal them.
No deployment evidence. Every method in the corpus is validated by simulation or a single case study. The phased sequence above is designed to generate our own evidence precisely because the literature does not supply it.
No cost model. The archive contains no capital cost, integration cost or change-management analysis. The business case must be built from vendor quotation and internal estimate, not from these documents.
A single structural dependency. Explainable reinforcement learning rests on one 2022 conference paper (13). If that approach does not transfer, the architecture still functions — it simply stops at Phase 3, retaining the deterministic planner and the explanation layer while forgoing the learned controller. The blueprint is deliberately built so that this outcome is a reduced benefit rather than a failed programme.
7. Conclusion
The scattered fragments inherited from the departed engineer do combine, but not by selecting a winner. They combine by assigning each method to the layer where its failure mode is least costly: constraints where violation is unacceptable, learning where adaptivity pays, explanation where trust is earned, and human authority above all of it. Task 5 packages this blueprint as an executive recommendation.
Layer | Function | Evidence base
L5 — Governance & human oversight | Planner and operator authority: accept, amend or override any schedule. Override reasons logged and fed back as training signal. Safety interlocks outside the learned policy. | 25, 16, 6
L4 — Explanation layer | Every released schedule carries a reason: feature attribution for the drivers of a sequence, and counterfactuals stating what would have had to change for the alternative the planner expected. | 8, 4, 13
L3 — Reactive policy (real time) | DRL agent adjusts within the shift envelope in response to price movements, delays and breakdowns. Multi-agent where furnace, caster and mill must coordinate. Acts only inside the feasible band set by L2. | 9, 21, 5, 20, 31
L2 — Deterministic planner (shift horizon) | MILP or metaheuristic produces the auditable base schedule and, critically, the hard feasibility envelope: minimum heating time, maximum residence time, charging capacity, no-idle and deterioration constraints. | 1, 22, 23, 28, 12, 15, 17
L1 — Prediction & forecasting | Surrogate models for energy per tonne and process parameters; time-series forecasts of job release and by-product gas availability; robust bounds where forecasts are weak. | 14, 3, 24, 2, 29
L0 — Digital twin & data foundation | IoT instrumentation and a twin of the reheating furnaces providing state, thermal behaviour and a safe environment in which L3 can be trained and any schedule pre-validated before release. | 10, 19, 27, 26
Tension from Task 3 | Resolution in the blueprint
Model-based optimisation vs learned policy | Both, at different horizons. L2 produces the shift plan and the feasibility envelope; L3 optimises within it intra-shift. Guarantees are preserved where they matter (feasibility) and abandoned where they are not achievable anyway (reaction to price and disturbance).
Proactive robustness vs reactive rescheduling | Robust bounds are applied only where forecasts are weak (L1), rather than as blanket slack. Elsewhere the reactive layer absorbs variance, so the plant does not pay for protection it does not need.
Energy quantity vs energy cost | Made explicit rather than assumed. Physical consumption enters as a constrained quantity with a floor set by metallurgy; cost is the objective optimised above that floor. The organisation sets the exchange rate between the two, and it is visible in the explanation layer.
Performance vs explainability | Explanation is a layer, not a property of the model, so it does not constrain the choice of controller. Counterfactual explanation is used because it answers the planner's actual question — why not the schedule I expected.
High-fidelity twin vs data-driven surrogate | Both, at different fidelities. The twin (L0) is the validation and training environment where error is cheap; surrogates (L1) supply fast predictions inside the optimisation loop where latency matters.
Constraint | Physical basis | Role in the architecture | Source
Minimum heating time per slab | Metallurgical: the slab must reach rolling temperature throughout its section. | Hard constraint in L2; the L3 agent cannot select an action that violates it. | 10, 15, 23
Maximum residence time | Excess time in furnace causes scale loss, decarburisation and quality rejection. | Hard upper bound; makes unlimited load-shifting to cheap price windows infeasible. | 23, 10
Furnace charging capacity and billet geometry | Physical: slab width and dimensions determine how many can be charged and in what order. | Feasibility mask on sequencing decisions. | 15, 10
Deterioration of heating efficiency | Reheat time is not constant; efficiency degrades with operating condition. | Time-varying parameter supplied by L1 to L2, not a fixed coefficient. | 23, 2
Ladle turnover and interface timing | Upstream ironmaking–steelmaking interface constrains when material arrives. | Coupling constraint between furnace schedule and upstream dispatch. | 18, 12
By-product gas availability | Internal fuel supply fluctuates and interacts with the external energy purchase decision. | Forecast input to the L3 cost objective. | 24

Task 5 — Final Report & Strategic Storytelling
Executive briefing · Energy-efficient intelligent scheduling for furnace operations · AIDA structure
Executive summary
We hold 31 peer-reviewed studies on energy-efficient furnace scheduling, inherited rather than commissioned. Analysed systematically, they support one recommendation: build a layered scheduling system in which deterministic optimisation sets the metallurgical envelope, a learned controller optimises cost inside it, and an explanation layer makes every decision answerable to the planner. Deploy it in phases, with the transparent components first. The first phase is low-risk, self-contained and delivers measurable energy reduction before any machine-learning component is introduced.
A — Attention: what energy is costing us
Steel is among the most energy-intensive industries in existence, and the literature we hold is unambiguous that the cost pressure is structural rather than cyclical. Document 9 opens by describing an industry facing rising energy costs alongside a decarbonisation imperative, and identifies scheduling complexity and interdependency as the obstacle to responding. Document 21 frames participation in demand response as a necessity for heavy industry rather than an option.
The relevant point for this organisation is not that energy is expensive. It is that a measurable share of what we spend is not consumed by metallurgy at all. It is consumed by idle furnace time, by slabs held longer than they need to be, by charging sequences chosen for convenience, and by heats run during expensive price windows when they could have run during cheap ones. Document 28 reports that eliminating idle machine time alone reduced total consumed energy by 29.57% in its test set, at a makespan penalty of 0.12%. That figure comes from a laboratory benchmark and is not a forecast for our plant. It is an indication of the order of magnitude of what scheduling discipline, rather than capital equipment, can recover.
We currently cannot state our own equivalent figure, because we have never measured it.
I — Interest: the capability now exists
Three developments in the last five years have made this tractable where previously it was not.
Digital twins have made the furnace visible. Document 10 builds a high-fidelity twin of parallel walking-beam reheating furnaces, arguing that the absence of digital representation is precisely why optimisation schemes have historically deviated so badly in implementation. Document 19 extends this across rolling stages to break the information silos between them.
Reinforcement learning has made schedules responsive. Document 9 demonstrates a deep reinforcement learning method that schedules a steel plant against electricity spot prices under genuine uncertainty from both prices and on-site renewable generation. Document 21 coordinates multiple production agents for demand response. This is a capability no classical scheduling model in our archive possesses.
Prediction has become accurate enough to optimise against. Document 14 predicts heat energy consumption per tonne in a steel rolling reheating furnace to 94.7% accuracy using a genetic-algorithm-optimised neural network trained on real production data.
Individually, none of these is a strategy. Combined, they describe a plant that knows its own thermal state, can predict the energy cost of a proposed schedule, and can adjust that schedule as prices and disruptions move.
D — Desire: why this will be trusted rather than overridden
The reason to expect this to work where previous automation efforts have disappointed is that we are treating adoption as an engineering requirement rather than a communications exercise.
The literature is explicit about the failure mode. Document 13 states that machine-learning models are perceived as black boxes, which reduces user trust in the decisions a planning system proposes. Document 6 describes algorithms that produce results that are highly accurate yet incomprehensible, and argues that a transparent process is what strengthens trust between people and machines. A schedule that planners do not understand is a schedule they will override, and an overridden schedule delivers nothing regardless of how good it was.
Our design answers this in three ways. First, the metallurgical constraints — minimum heating time, maximum residence time, charging capacity — are enforced structurally, outside the learned component. The system is not permitted to trade product quality for energy cost, because those actions do not exist in its option set. Second, every schedule is released with an explanation, using the counterfactual approach of document 8, which answers the planner's real question: what would have had to be different for the schedule I expected to have been chosen. Third, planner authority to amend or reject is retained permanently, consistent with document 25, which asks whether process industries should pursue artificial intelligence or intelligence augmentation, and with document 16, which builds scheduling around operator state rather than despite it.
The sequencing reinforces this. The transparent, deterministic components are deployed first and run in advisory mode. Planners work with machine-generated reasoning for a year before any learned controller is introduced.
A — Action: what we are asking for
Risks we are accepting
The evidence base is simulation-heavy. Nearly every method in the archive is validated in simulation or a single case study, not in sustained production. Phase 1 exists to generate our own evidence before significant commitment.
Explainable reinforcement learning rests on thin ground. A single 2022 conference paper connects explanation techniques to learned production controllers. If this does not transfer to our environment, the programme stops after Phase 3 and we retain a transparent deterministic planner — a reduced benefit, not a failure.
Benchmark figures are not forecasts. The energy reductions cited in this briefing come from other plants and test instances. They justify investigation; they do not justify a committed target. A target should be set after Phase 1.
The decision in one sentence
Approve a six-month, low-risk measurement phase that tells us what our furnace scheduling is actually costing us, and settle now how we intend to weigh energy consumed against energy paid for — because every subsequent decision follows from those two answers.
Decision required | Horizon | Why now
1 | Approve Phase 1: instrument the reheating furnaces and build the digital twin. Establish our energy baseline in GJ per tonne. | 0–6 months | We cannot set a target, build a business case or measure success without a baseline. This is the binding prerequisite for everything else.
2 | Settle the objective. Decide, at board level, how physical energy reduction and energy cost reduction are to be weighted against each other. | Immediate | These objectives conflict. Load-shifting to cheap price windows can increase physical consumption. Engineering cannot resolve this; it is a management decision and it determines what we build.
3 | Fund Phase 2: the deterministic planner, in advisory mode alongside current practice. | 6–12 months | Self-contained, fully auditable, no black-box component. Captures the idle-time and sequencing gains on its own and is the fallback position if later phases do not proceed.
4 | Name an owner and a planner working group. | Immediate | The evidence is clear that adoption, not algorithm quality, is the dominant risk. The explanation layer must be designed with the people who will use it.
5 | Commission an external cost estimate. | 0–3 months | Our archive contains no capital, integration or change-management costs. The business case cannot be completed from internal analysis alone.
